::: {.callout-tip title="Learning objectives" icon="false"}
After this lecture (and Lab 3) you can:

1. **state** the encoder–decoder framework — encoder, decoder, similarity, loss — and place any embedding method inside it;
2. **derive** the DeepWalk/node2vec objective from walk co-occurrence through the softmax to negative sampling, defining every symbol along the way;
3. **explain** node2vec's $p$ and $q$ as a BFS↔DFS dial and predict their effect on a given graph;
4. **connect** random-walk embeddings to matrix factorization (the NetMF result, statement only) and use it to reason about what they can and cannot capture;
5. **enumerate** the four limitations of shallow embeddings — no sharing, transductive-only, feature-blind, $O(|\mathcal{V}|d)$ parameters — and match each to the scenario where it bites;
6. **contrast** learned embeddings with label propagation on the same task, and say when the no-learning baseline wins.
:::

## The year the surfers learned to write

In 2013, a small team at Google showed that if you feed a neural network billions of
sentences and ask it to guess each word's neighbors, the network is forced to invent a
**vector for every word** — and those vectors turn out to carry meaning: countries
cluster together, verb tenses align along one direction, and the arithmetic
*king − man + woman* famously lands near *queen*. The system was called word2vec
[Mikolov et al., 2013](https://arxiv.org/abs/1301.3781), and it rearranged natural
language processing in about a year.

Graph researchers read that paper with a specific kind of greed, and within a year
had committed the field's most productive act of theft. Their problem was
Week 2's cliffhanger: hand-crafted features had just hit a ceiling — statistics were
topic-blind, and the informative thing, *position*, was being butchered into one-hot
community ids. What they wanted was a **learned, continuous vector per node**. What
word2vec needed to provide one per word was only a corpus of sentences.

::: {.predict}
**Commit before you look.** word2vec learns from sentences — linear sequences of
tokens. If you had to manufacture "sentences" out of a graph so the same code runs
unchanged, what would a sentence be?

::: {.predict-answer}
**A random walk.** Start anywhere, follow random edges, write down the nodes you visit:
a linear sequence of tokens in which co-occurrence means proximity — exactly what a
sentence is to word2vec. That one-line answer is the
[DeepWalk paper (2014)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1403.6652), one of the
most influential ideas in graph ML, and you already own every ingredient: you built the
walk machinery for PageRank last week.
:::
:::

{{< include ../assets/figures/fig-w3-hero.html >}}

Notice what the pairs in the figure preserve and what they discard: the pair (E,C)
appears twice — *frequency of co-occurrence* is the signal — while everything about
edge identity, direction of travel, and global position is thrown away. This lecture is
about what survives that compression, why it is enough to beat every feature you built
last week, and where it runs out.

Since we are inheriting word2vec's machinery wholesale, spend three paragraphs
knowing what you inherit. word2vec is actually *two* models: **CBOW** predicts a
center word from the average of its context, **skip-gram** predicts each context word
from the center. Skip-gram is the one graph methods took, for a reason that matters
here more than in text: averaging a context before predicting (CBOW) blurs rare
nodes into their popular neighbors, while skip-gram gives every individual
co-occurrence its own gradient — and graphs, with their heavy-tailed degrees (Week 1),
have a far worse rare-versus-popular imbalance than vocabulary does.

Second
inheritance: word2vec keeps **two vectors per word** — a center table and a context
table — because one object plays two statistical roles ("how I behave as a focus" vs
"how I behave as company"); using one table forces $\mathbf{z}_u^\top \mathbf{z}_u$
terms into the objective, which pressures every vector toward a large norm for no
semantic reason. Graph implementations follow suit, then typically keep only the
center table (as our lab will; the homework asks you to think about why that is
safe).

Third inheritance, and the least advertised: word2vec *subsamples frequent
words* — it randomly deletes a fraction of "the" and "of" occurrences before
windowing, precisely because ultra-frequent tokens flood $\mathcal{D}$ with
uninformative pairs. The graph translation writes itself: hubs are the stop-words of
a network. DeepWalk quietly benefits from the walk dynamics already damping this
(a walk *leaves* a hub in one step), node2vec's $p$ knob modulates it further, and
when you meet "degree bias" for the fourth time this semester, you now know the NLP
world solved its version of it in the same 2013 paper we are borrowing everything
else from.

**Roadmap.** (1) A template that organizes this week and the next three: encoder,
decoder, similarity, loss. (2) Walks as similarity — watch the training data being
manufactured. (3) The objective, derived honestly: softmax, why it is unaffordable, and
the negative-sampling rescue. (4) node2vec: two knobs that steer what "nearby" means.
(5) Training, watched live — and what the optimum secretly is (a matrix factorization).
(6) Using embeddings: classification and link prediction done right. (7) The
no-learning baseline, the four limitations, and the door to GNNs.

::: {.callout-note title="Recap — what this lecture assumes" collapse="true"}
- **Week 2**: random walks and PageRank's surfer; the Cora measurement — structural statistics 19%, + Louvain-community one-hots 62%; homophily (Week 1's glossary): connected nodes tend to be alike.
- **From your ML course**: logistic regression / sigmoid $\sigma(x) = 1/(1+e^{-x})$; softmax; SGD; what a loss function is.
- **From Week 1**: graphs as `edge_index`; the ordering trap — features must not depend on node numbering. (Today's encoder *looks like* it violates this; §5 resolves the tension.)
:::

## 1. One template for the next four weeks

Strip any node-embedding method to its skeleton and four decisions remain:

{{< include ../assets/figures/fig-w3-encdec.html >}}

::: {#def-w03-encdec .definition name="Encoder–decoder template"}
A node-embedding method is a choice of four components:

- an <span class="term" data-def="Encoder: the function mapping a node id to its vector. This week it is pure table lookup — ENC(u) = Z[u], one trainable row per node. In Week 6 the encoder becomes a neural network that computes the vector from features and neighbors.">**encoder**</span> mapping each node to a vector. This week it is the simplest thing that could work: a **lookup table** $\mathbf{Z} \in \mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{V}| \times d}$, one free row $\mathbf{z}_u = \mathbf{Z}[u]$ per node, $d \approx 64$–$256$. No computation — the parameters *are* the answer;
- a **decoder** turning two vectors into a score for the pair. This week: the dot
  product $\mathbf{z}_u^\top \mathbf{z}_v$ (sometimes passed through a sigmoid);
- a **similarity** $S(u,v)$: what the graph says the score *should* be — the
  design decision that actually distinguishes methods;
- a **loss** measuring the disagreement, driving SGD on the table $\mathbf{Z}$.

Read any new embedding paper by filling in these four slots first — almost always
only the similarity is genuinely new.
:::

The filing cabinet, which we will keep filling until Week 6 — memorize its columns,
not its rows, because the columns are the questions you ask of every new method:

| method | encoder | decoder | similarity $S(u,v)$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| adjacency factorization | lookup | $\mathbf{z}_u^\top\mathbf{z}_v$ | $\mathbf{A}[u,v]$ |
| **DeepWalk** (2014) | lookup | softmax of dots | walk co-occurrence |
| **node2vec** (2016) | lookup | softmax of dots | *biased*-walk co-occurrence |
| TransE (Week 4) | lookup | $-\|\mathbf{z}_h + \mathbf{r} - \mathbf{z}_t\|$ | typed triples |
| GCN (Week 6) | *a neural network* | task-dependent | task labels |

Why prefer walk co-occurrence over the obvious $S = \mathbf{A}$? Because adjacency is
brittle and shallow: it declares $u$ and $v$ "similar" only if they share an edge, and
two members of the same tight community with no direct tie get $S = 0$ — the same
score as total strangers. On a sparse graph that zero is almost everywhere — Cora's
adjacency is 99.9% zeros, so a factorization of $\mathbf{A}$ spends its capacity
modeling absence. Walks fix this with the multi-hop, probabilistic notion of
neighborhood you already trust from PageRank: nodes are similar if a short random walk
from one *tends to reach* the other — a similarity that is dense where it matters
(within communities) and graded rather than binary.

## 2. Manufacturing the training data

Everything the loss will ever know about the graph is produced by this pipeline: run
walks, slide a window, count pairs. Watch the raw material being made:

{{< include ../assets/d3/w3-walks.html >}}

Formally: fix a walk length $K$ and a window size $w$. Run $\gamma$ walks from every
node. For each walk $(v_1, \ldots, v_K)$ and each position $i$, emit the pairs
$(v_i, v_j)$ for all $j \neq i$ with $|i - j| \le w$, and call the multiset of all
emitted pairs $\mathcal{D}$. This is the entire data pipeline of DeepWalk
[Perozzi et al., 2014](https://arxiv.org/abs/1403.6652), and since Lab 3 has you
build it, here it is as a procedure — @alg-w03-corpus is exercises 1 and 2 of the
lab, step for step:

::: {#alg-w03-corpus .algorithm name="Walk Corpus → Skip-Gram Pairs (DeepWalk)"}
Manufactures the training multiset $\mathcal{D}$ of (center, context) pairs from truncated random walks.

**Input:** graph $G = (\mathcal{V}, \mathcal{E})$; walks per node $\gamma$; walk length $K$; window $w$; seed $s$. **Output:** multiset $\mathcal{D}$ of (center, context) pairs.

1. rng ← Random($s$); $W$ ← empty list; $\mathcal{D}$ ← empty multiset
2. **for** round $= 1, \ldots, \gamma$ **do**
3. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;**for** each start node $v \in \mathcal{V}$, in sorted order, **do**
4. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;walk ← $(v)$
5. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;**while** $|\text{walk}| < K$ and last(walk) has neighbors **do**
6. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;append a neighbor of last(walk), chosen uniformly by rng
7. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;append walk to $W$
8. **end for**
9. **for** each walk $(v_1, \ldots, v_K) \in W$ and each position $i$ **do**
10. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;**for** each $j \neq i$ with $|i - j| \le w$: add $(v_i, v_j)$ to $\mathcal{D}$
11. **end for**
12. **return** $\mathcal{D}$
:::

Three notes on the listing, because each one is a lab assert. The single seeded rng
and the sorted node order are the determinism contract — same seed, same corpus,
always. The **while** guard handles dead ends: a walk stuck at an isolated node
simply stops early. And the pair count is exact: a full-length walk emits
$2wK - w(w{+}1)$ pairs, so $|\mathcal{D}| = |\mathcal{V}| \cdot \gamma \cdot \bigl(2wK - w(w{+}1)\bigr)$
when no walk ends early — exercise 2 checks your code against this closed form. The
empirical similarity is then simply

$$
S(u, v) \;=\; \#\{(u,v) \in \mathcal{D}\}
$$ {#eq-w03-simcount}

where $\#\{(u,v) \in \mathcal{D}\}$ counts how many times the ordered pair $(u, v)$
occurs in the multiset $\mathcal{D}$ — the matrix you watched fill up in Figure 1. It
is a blurred, multi-hop version of adjacency: row $u$ resembles row $u$ of
$\mathbf{A}$ smeared over $w$ hops, with counts where 0/1 entries used to be.

What, exactly, does the blur compute? In expectation, a window-$w$ co-occurrence
from center $u$ is a step of the random walk iterated between 1 and $w$ times — so
the expected similarity matrix is a mixture of transition-matrix powers:

$$
\mathbb{E}\bigl[S\bigr] \;\propto\; \frac{1}{w} \sum_{i=1}^{w} \bigl(\mathbf{D}^{-1}\mathbf{A}\bigr)^{i}
$$ {#eq-w03-expwalk}

where $S$ is the co-occurrence-count matrix of @eq-w03-simcount, $\mathbf{A}$ is the
adjacency matrix, $\mathbf{D}$ the diagonal degree matrix — so $\mathbf{D}^{-1}\mathbf{A}$
is Week 2's random-walk transition matrix — and its $i$-th power moves the walker $i$
steps. You have held every ingredient of @eq-w03-expwalk since Week 1: powers of an
adjacency-like matrix count walk structure, the $\mathbf{D}^{-1}$ makes them
probabilities, and $w$ sets how many powers get mixed in. This is also the cleanest
way to *see* the window knob's meaning before we tune it later: $w = 1$ recovers
(normalized) adjacency; $w = 10$ mixes in tenth powers, which on a small-world graph
(Week 1 again) already reach most of a community — hence "large $w$ embeds
community, small $w$ embeds adjacency." The pipeline's stochasticity is just Monte
Carlo over this expectation; the NetMF result in the next section will replace the
Monte Carlo with the exact matrix and lose nothing but the randomness.

One more property deserves explicit notice, because it is a Week-1 promise being
kept: the pipeline is **permutation-fair**. Renumber the nodes and rerun; the walk
*distribution* is identical up to renaming, so the expected statistics — and hence
the geometry the fixed point prescribes — follow the renaming exactly (equivariance),
while every graph-level readout of them is unchanged (invariance). The subtlety
confessed here, as promised in Week 1: any *single* seeded run breaks ties through
the numbering (the RNG consumes nodes in some order), so two renumbered runs differ
by more than renaming — but by *sampling noise only*, which vanishes in the limit
that the theory describes. Storage still is not information; it just gets one vote
per finite sample.

## 3. The objective, derived honestly

We want the embedding of a center node to *predict its contexts*. The maximum-likelihood
way to say that: model the probability of seeing context $v$ given center $u$ as a
softmax over all nodes, and maximize it over the observed pairs:

$$
\max_{\mathbf{Z}}\;
\sum_{(u,v) \in \mathcal{D}} \log \Pr(v \mid u),
\qquad
\Pr(v \mid u) \;=\;
\frac{\exp(\mathbf{z}_u^\top \mathbf{z}_v)}{\sum_{n \in \mathcal{V}} \exp(\mathbf{z}_u^\top \mathbf{z}_n)} .
$$ {#eq-w03-softmax}

::: {.callout-important title="Every symbol of the softmax objective, defined — read this box like a contract" icon="false"}
This formula has appeared on this course's midterm before, written sloppily, and it
cost everyone points. The precise inventory: $\mathcal{D}$ is the multiset of
(center, context) pairs emitted by the walk-and-window pipeline of §2 — *it is data,
fixed before training*. $\mathbf{z}_u \in \mathbb{R}^d$ is row $u$ of the trainable
table $\mathbf{Z}$. The sum in the denominator runs over **all** $|\mathcal{V}|$ nodes
— that is what makes it a probability, and what makes it unaffordable. (Faithful
implementations keep *two* tables — a center table and a context table, $\mathbf{z}_u^\top \mathbf{z}'_v$
— exactly as word2vec does; we suppress the prime until the NetMF box, where it
matters.)
:::

The denominator is the whole problem: every SGD step on every pair touches all
$|\mathcal{V}|$ embeddings — $O(|\mathcal{V}|)$ per pair, hopeless at
$|\mathcal{V}| = 10^8$ (a single epoch over a billion pairs would cost $10^{17}$
embedding touches — years of compute for one pass). word2vec's escape
[Mikolov et al., 2013](https://arxiv.org/abs/1310.4546), inherited verbatim by
DeepWalk and node2vec, is **negative sampling**: stop normalizing, start
discriminating. For each real pair, draw $k$ fake contexts from a noise distribution
$P_n$ and train a logistic classifier to tell them apart:

$$
\mathcal{L} \;=\;
\sum_{(u,v) \in \mathcal{D}}
\Bigl[
\log \sigma(\mathbf{z}_u^\top \mathbf{z}_v)
\;+\;
\sum_{i=1}^{k} \mathbb{E}_{n_i \sim P_n} \log \sigma(-\mathbf{z}_u^\top \mathbf{z}_{n_i})
\Bigr]
$$ {#eq-w03-sgns}

where — $\mathcal{D}$ is the pair multiset manufactured by @alg-w03-corpus;
$\sigma(x) = 1/(1+e^{-x})$ is the logistic sigmoid; $k$ is the number of negatives
per real pair; the $n_i$ are the fake contexts, drawn from the noise distribution
$P_n$ over nodes; and $\mathbf{z}_u, \mathbf{z}_v, \mathbf{z}_{n_i} \in \mathbb{R}^d$
are rows of the trainable table. Maximize: pull real pairs together (first term),
push $k$ random impostors apart (second). Cost per pair: $O(k)$, with
$k \approx 5$–$20$.

::: {#def-w03-negsampling .definition name="Negative sampling"}
Replace a softmax's classify-against-everyone objective by binary discrimination:
for every observed pair, train the score to accept the real pair and reject $k$
fakes drawn from a noise distribution $P_n$, as in @eq-w03-sgns. Cost per pair drops
from $O(|\mathcal{V}|)$ to $O(k)$. Read it as a bargain: give up computing exact
probabilities over all nodes, keep the geometry those probabilities would induce.
:::

The noise distribution is *not* uniform in practice — word2vec's choice:

$$
P_n(v) \;\propto\; \deg(v)^{3/4}
$$ {#eq-w03-noise}

where $P_n(v)$ is the probability that node $v$ is drawn as a fake context and
$\deg(v)$ is its degree — sample frequent/high-degree nodes as negatives more often,
or the model learns mostly that hubs exist (Pitfall 5 will return to this). Lab 3
keeps $P_n$ uniform — a deliberate simplification that costs little on the small,
degree-tame graphs you will train on there.

Take the gradient once by hand, because "one sigmoid pull, $k$ sigmoid pushes" should
be arithmetic to you, not poetry. The only calculus required is the sigmoid's
log-derivative:

$$
\frac{d}{ds}\log\sigma(s) \;=\; \sigma(-s) \;=\; 1 - \sigma(s)
$$ {#eq-w03-siggrad}

where $s$ is whatever score the loss feeds to $\log \sigma$ — here a dot product.
Applying @eq-w03-siggrad to each term of @eq-w03-sgns for a single pair:

$$
\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \mathbf{z}_u}
= \bigl(1 - \sigma(\mathbf{z}_u^\top \mathbf{z}_v)\bigr)\,\mathbf{z}_v
\;-\; \sum_{i=1}^{k} \sigma(\mathbf{z}_u^\top \mathbf{z}_{n_i})\,\mathbf{z}_{n_i}
$$ {#eq-w03-grad}

where the coefficient $1 - \sigma(\mathbf{z}_u^\top \mathbf{z}_v)$ is the *pull*
strength — how surprised the model still is by the real pair — and each
$\sigma(\mathbf{z}_u^\top \mathbf{z}_{n_i})$ is a *push* strength — how fooled it
currently is by negative $n_i$. The gradient for $\mathbf{z}_v$ is symmetric (pulled
toward $\mathbf{z}_u$ by the same surprise factor), and each negative is pushed away.
Assembled into a procedure, with the two tables the faithful implementation keeps,
this gradient is exactly what Lab 3's exercise 3 computes — @alg-w03-sgns is one
optimizer step of your `sgns_loss`:

::: {#alg-w03-sgns .algorithm name="One SGNS Update"}
Applies the gradient of @eq-w03-sgns for one observed pair, by gradient ascent.

**Input:** pair $(u, v) \in \mathcal{D}$; center table $\mathbf{Z}$ and context table $\mathbf{Z}'$; number of negatives $k$; noise distribution $P_n$; learning rate $\eta$. **Output:** updated rows $\mathbf{z}_u$, $\mathbf{z}'_v$, $\mathbf{z}'_{n_1}, \ldots, \mathbf{z}'_{n_k}$.

1. draw fake contexts $n_1, \ldots, n_k \sim P_n$
2. $g \leftarrow 1 - \sigma(\mathbf{z}_u^\top \mathbf{z}'_v)$ &nbsp;&nbsp;▹ pull strength
3. $\boldsymbol{\Delta} \leftarrow g\,\mathbf{z}'_v$; &nbsp; then $\mathbf{z}'_v \leftarrow \mathbf{z}'_v + \eta\, g\, \mathbf{z}_u$
4. **for** $i = 1, \ldots, k$ **do**
5. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;$h \leftarrow \sigma(\mathbf{z}_u^\top \mathbf{z}'_{n_i})$ &nbsp;&nbsp;▹ push strength
6. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;$\boldsymbol{\Delta} \leftarrow \boldsymbol{\Delta} - h\,\mathbf{z}'_{n_i}$; &nbsp; then $\mathbf{z}'_{n_i} \leftarrow \mathbf{z}'_{n_i} - \eta\, h\, \mathbf{z}_u$
7. **end for**
8. $\mathbf{z}_u \leftarrow \mathbf{z}_u + \eta\, \boldsymbol{\Delta}$
9. **return**
:::

The primes mark the context table — the "two vectors per node" inheritance from the
opening; the lab's `train_sgns` keeps both and returns the center table. The
accumulator $\boldsymbol{\Delta}$ exists so that every pull and push is computed from
the *pre-update* vectors, as a simultaneous gradient step requires. Cost: $k + 1$
dot products and $k + 2$ row updates — $O(kd)$ per pair, independent of
$|\mathcal{V}|$.

Numbers, in $d = 2$ with one negative: let
$\mathbf{z}_u = (1, 0)$, $\mathbf{z}_v = (0.5, 0.5)$, $\mathbf{z}_n = (0.8, -0.2)$.
Then $s_{uv} = 0.5$, $\sigma(0.5) \approx 0.62$, so the pull coefficient is $0.38$;
$s_{un} = 0.8$, $\sigma(0.8) \approx 0.69$ — a *hard* negative, big push. Gradient on
$\mathbf{z}_u$: $0.38 \cdot (0.5, 0.5) - 0.69 \cdot (0.8, -0.2) = (-0.36, 0.33)$ —
the update drags $u$ away from the impostor more strongly than toward the friend,
because right now the impostor scores higher. Two structural facts fall out of the
formula for free: gradients vanish as the model gets confident (both coefficients
$\to 0$ — SGNS self-anneals, no schedule heroics required), and every update touches
exactly $k + 2$ rows of the tables — the locality that makes a 100-million-node
embedding trainable at all.

Is negative sampling just a hack? No — it has a precise fixed point
([Levy & Goldberg, 2014](https://papers.nips.cc/paper/5477-neural-word-embedding-as-implicit-matrix-factorization);
[Qiu et al., 2018](https://arxiv.org/abs/1710.02971)), and the fixed point is a
familiar object:

::: {#prp-netmf .proposition name="What SGNS secretly optimizes (Levy–Goldberg 2014; NetMF 2018 — statement only)"}
With embedding dimension large enough, the SGNS objective is minimized when

$$
\mathbf{z}_u^\top \mathbf{z}'_v \;=\; \mathrm{PMI}(u, v) - \log k
\;=\; \log \frac{\#(u,v)\,|\mathcal{D}|}{\#(u)\,\#(v)} - \log k,
$$ {#eq-w03-netmf}

where — $\#(u,v)$ is the number of times the pair $(u,v)$ occurs in the corpus
$\mathcal{D}$; $\#(u) = \sum_x \#(u,x)$ and $\#(v) = \sum_x \#(x,v)$ are $u$'s total
count as a center and $v$'s as a context; $|\mathcal{D}|$ is the total number of
pairs; $k$ is the number of negatives; and $\mathrm{PMI}$, the pointwise mutual
information, *is* the log-ratio shown — how much more often the pair co-occurs than
independent draws would predict. In words: DeepWalk **implicitly factorizes** the
(shifted) PMI matrix of its walk co-occurrences — and the prime finally matters,
because the factorization is of the center table against the context table. NetMF
([Qiu et al., 2018](https://arxiv.org/abs/1710.02971)) computes this matrix in
closed form from $\mathbf{A}$ — powers of the transition matrix averaged over the
window, as in @eq-w03-expwalk — and factorizing it directly ("DeepWalk without the
walks") often *beats* DeepWalk. The optional reading has the derivation; on the exam
you need the statement and its uses.
:::

The statement earns its keep as a reasoning tool. Two immediate consequences: walk
embeddings see **only co-occurrence statistics** — two nodes with identical structural
roles on opposite sides of a large graph never co-occur, so they get unrelated vectors
(embeddings capture *homophily*, community-position, not *roles* — remember WL from
Week 2 captured the opposite); and the whole method is **spectral in disguise** — a
low-rank factorization of a fixed matrix, which is why the figure below could compute
"DeepWalk's answer" exactly, with no SGD at all.

The statement also organizes the *history*, which on exams and in interviews doubles
as a map of the design space. DeepWalk (2014) opened the era;
[**LINE** (2015)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1503.03578) asked
"why walk at all?" and optimized two explicit objectives instead — first-order
proximity (endpoints of an edge should be close: $S = \mathbf{A}$ with a logistic
loss) and second-order proximity (nodes with similar *neighborhoods* should be close)
— trading the walk's multi-hop blur for controllable, separately-trained notions of
similarity at hundred-million-edge scale. **node2vec** (2016) kept the walks and made
their bias a dial.

Then **NetMF** (2018) ended the era's theoretical innocence by
proving all of them — DeepWalk, LINE, node2vec, and their text ancestors — implicitly
factorize closed-form matrices, with LINE falling out as *exactly* DeepWalk at window
$w = 1$. Four papers, one filing-cabinet drawer: a similarity choice ($\mathbf{A}$,
blurred $\mathbf{A}$, biased-blurred $\mathbf{A}$), a shift, a factorization. When
you meet a "new" embedding method, your first question is now mechanical: *what
matrix does it factorize?* — and the answer usually deflates the novelty by half
while clarifying the method entirely.

## 4. node2vec: steering the walker

If similarity = "where my walks go", then *biasing the walks changes the geometry of
the embedding space*. [node2vec (2016)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1607.00653) adds
exactly two knobs to the walker. Standing at $v$, having arrived from $t$, the
walker weighs each candidate next step $x$ by

$$
\alpha_{pq}(t, x) \;=\;
\begin{cases}
1/p & \text{if } d(t, x) = 0 \quad \text{(return to } t\text{)}\\
1 & \text{if } d(t, x) = 1 \quad \text{(a common neighbor of } t \text{ and } v\text{)}\\
1/q & \text{if } d(t, x) = 2 \quad \text{(farther from } t\text{)}
\end{cases}
$$ {#eq-w03-pq}

where $d(t, x)$ is the graph distance from the previous node $t$ to the candidate
$x$ — necessarily 0, 1, or 2, since $x$ neighbors the current node $v$; $p$ is the
**return** parameter (large $p$ discourages stepping back); $q$ is the **in-out**
parameter (small $q$ pushes the walk outward); and the weights $\alpha_{pq}$ are
normalized over $v$'s neighbors to give transition probabilities.

{{< include ../assets/figures/fig-w3-pq.html >}}

Low $q$ makes walks range far — a depth-first temperament that makes co-occurrence
mean "same region", grouping **communities** (homophily). High $q$ with low $p$ keeps
walks orbiting their origin — breadth-first — so co-occurrence statistics fingerprint
the *local* neighborhood shape, nudging embeddings toward **structural equivalence**
(hubs near hubs, bridges near bridges), at least at small scales. The paper's own
showpiece made the contrast visual: the Les Misérables character network embedded
twice, once clustering by *social circle* (who shares scenes), once by *narrative
role* (hubs with hubs, peripherals with peripherals) — same graph, same algorithm,
two legitimate geometries, chosen by two numbers. Don't take the
adjectives on faith — measure them:

{{< include ../assets/d3/w3-pq.html >}}

Make the bias concrete with one full hand computation, because the midterm's
node2vec question is always this computation with different numbers. On the cast
graph, suppose the walker stepped $A \to C$ (so $t = A$, current $v = C$) with
$p = 4$, $q = 0.5$. $C$'s neighbors are $A, B, E, F$. Classify each against $t = A$
using @eq-w03-pq:
$A$ is the way back (weight $1/p = 0.25$); $B$ is a neighbor of $A$ (weight $1$);
$E$ and $F$ are not adjacent to $A$ (weight $1/q = 2$ each). Normalizing over
$0.25 + 1 + 2 + 2 = 5.25$: the walker returns to $A$ with probability $\approx 0.05$,
sidesteps to $B$ with $\approx 0.19$, and pushes outward to $E$ or $F$ with
$\approx 0.38$ each — three-quarters of the probability mass is *escaping $A$'s
orbit*, which is the DFS temperament in one row of arithmetic. Recompute with
$p = 0.5, q = 4$ and the same row becomes $0.5, 1, 0.25, 0.25$ over $2.0$ — half the
mass now points straight back home. Two knobs, one normalization, and you can predict
a corpus's character before generating it.

One honest caveat the original paper is often paraphrased past: the walker is
second-order (it remembers one step back), so this is a nudge, not a guarantee — truly
role-based embeddings need different machinery
([struc2vec](https://arxiv.org/abs/1704.03165), [GraphWave](https://arxiv.org/abs/1710.10321)
— mentioned, not examined). What *is* exam-fair: given a graph and a task, predict which $(p, q)$ regime
helps, and defend it in the BFS/DFS vocabulary.

## 5. Training, watched live

You have now derived everything in the loop: sample a pair from $\mathcal{D}$, one
sigmoid pull, $k$ sigmoid pushes, repeat. Here is that exact loop, running in your
browser on the karate club, with $d = 2$ so that the embedding space needs no
projection to be seen:

{{< include ../assets/d3/w3-embed.html >}}

Two things to notice while it runs. First, the training never sees labels — the
factions emerge because walk co-occurrence *is* community structure (§3's consequence,
live). Second, node ordering never enters: rename every member and the same pairs are
sampled, the same geometry forms, merely with rows of $\mathbf{Z}$ permuted — the
Week 1 trap is dodged because the table is *indexed* by node, not *shaped* by ordering.
The permutation-invariance bill does come due — but at test time, not train time
(limitation 2 below).

While the auto-run plays, narrate the phases to yourself, because each one is a
statement about the loss landscape. The first few hundred pairs barely move anything
— random vectors score near zero, both sigmoid coefficients sit near one-half, and
pulls and pushes nearly cancel. Then the phase change: some pair of frequently
co-walking members drifts together by chance, their mutual pulls compound, their
shared negatives push the same directions, and a *cluster nucleates* — after which
growth is fast, because joining an existing cluster is downhill for every member the
walks associate with it.

Last, the slow endgame: clusters formed, gradients small,
points shuffling within their blobs while boundary members 2 and 8 wander the strait
between the camps — their walk statistics genuinely straddle both, so *no* stable
position exists for them except the middle, and that indecision is correct. You have
just watched non-convex optimization behave well for a graph-shaped reason:
homophily makes the good minima wide.

And because @prp-netmf says the destination of all this SGD is a fixed factorization,
we can skip the training entirely and compute where the points *must* end up:

{{< include ../assets/figures/fig-w3-embedding.html >}}

The static figure is the widget's asymptote: the PPMI matrix of real walk
co-occurrences — *positive* PMI, meaning @eq-w03-netmf's log-ratio with every
negative entry clipped to zero, the standard cure for the $-\infty$ that
never-co-occurring pairs would produce — factorized, two dimensions kept. Compare where the ringed boundary members sit in both
— training and factorization agree that members 2 and 8 live between the camps, which
is the same verdict the Fiedler vector delivered last week. Three different algorithms,
one geometric truth: **position in this graph is a low-dimensional, learnable thing.**

### Choosing the knobs, and knowing what each one means

The pipeline has five hyperparameters, and — unusually for deep-learning-adjacent
methods — each has a *semantic* reading, so tuning them is reasoning, not grid
search. Read the table column by column; it is the lecture-hall artifact worth
photographing today:

| knob | semantic reading | typical setting |
|---|---|---|
| dimension $d$ | the rank of the factorization (@prp-netmf): how much of the co-occurrence spectrum you keep — communities are low-rank structure, walk noise is high-rank | $64$–$256$; Q4 shows why more can hurt |
| window $w$ | the *scale of "nearby"*: small $w$ ≈ sharp, local adjacency; large $w$ blurs toward "same region" — on Cora, raising $w$ merges sub-topics into topics | the single most task-sensitive knob — the natural Part-C investigation in HW1 |
| walks $\gamma$, length $K$ | pure variance control: more corpus, less sampling noise around the same expected statistics | DeepWalk's famous $80 \times 40$ is generous overkill for small graphs; the lab's lean settings deliberately are not |
| negatives $k$ | enters @eq-w03-netmf as the shift $-\log k$: larger $k$ demands more evidence before a pair scores positive (a regularizer), and linearly buys gradient quality per pair | $5$–$20$ |
| learning rate, epochs | ordinary SGD lore, plus one graph-specific note you measure in the lab: past the point where communities form, further epochs mostly fit walk-sampling noise | the lab's Adam defaults; stop early |

When a paper reports beating DeepWalk, your first question is now professional
reflex: *at whose hyperparameters?*

### Living with embeddings in production

Because shallow embeddings are cheap and effective, they get deployed — and then the
lookup-table nature bites operationally in ways worth knowing before your first
on-call. **Retraining and alignment:** the loss is rotation-invariant (Pitfall 2), so
Tuesday's retrain produces vectors incompatible with Monday's — any downstream system
that cached similarities or trained a model on the old coordinates silently degrades.
Fixes: align successive runs with orthogonal Procrustes (find the rotation minimizing
$\|\mathbf{Z}_{\text{new}}\mathbf{R} - \mathbf{Z}_{\text{old}}\|$ — one line of code
via the SVD, the singular value decomposition your linear algebra course called the
master factorization), or warm-start training from the previous table.

**Drift monitoring:** the graph
changes under the model; track a fixed probe set's neighborhood overlap between
versions, and alert when it drops — embarrassingly few teams do.

**Cold start:** new
entities have no row (limitation 2); production stopgaps include averaging the
embeddings of a new node's first neighbors (surprisingly strong), keeping a "fresh
node" model on features alone, and scheduled fold-in mini-trainings. All three are
patches on a structural hole, which is the honest sales pitch for Week 6. And the
counterpoint, because engineering is trade-offs: when your graph is static-ish, your
entities stable, and your latency budget tight, a precomputed embedding table served
from a feature store is *faster and simpler than any neural encoder will ever be* —
shallow methods still run large production recommenders for exactly this reason.

## 6. Using the vectors

Embeddings are middleware — their value is what the next model does with them.

**Node classification.** Feed $\mathbf{z}_u$ to logistic regression. This is Lab 2's
pipeline with the hand-crafted features swapped for learned ones, and it is the third
rung of our running Cora measurement: statistics 19% → +community one-hots 62% →
**walk embeddings ≈ 68%** (you will produce this number yourself in Lab 3). The jump
over one-hots is exactly the value of *continuous, graded* position over hard
membership: boundary papers get boundary coordinates instead of a forced binary id —
and the six extra points are worth dwelling on for one more sentence, because of
*where* they come from: not from any information the one-hots lacked (both pipelines
see only structure), but from a better-shaped compression of the same information.
Representation quality is a real, separable axis from information content; that
distinction is half of what "representation learning" means, and this ladder is the
cleanest demonstration of it you will ever compute.

(One practical rite of passage awaits you in the lab: the probe only clears ~64% until
you L2-normalize the vectors — SGNS stores walk *frequency* in a vector's norm and
*position* in its direction, and the probe wants the direction.)

A word on *how* we measure the classification claim, because the protocol is a
transferable skill. The standard instrument is the **frozen linear probe**: freeze the
embeddings, train only logistic regression on top, report its accuracy. Why not
fine-tune, or use a stronger classifier? Because the question is about the
*representation*, and a powerful classifier can compensate for a mediocre
representation — the probe's weakness is the point, it makes the embedding do the
work. Why linear specifically? Linear separability is the operational meaning of
"the classes form separated regions in this space." The two hygiene rules you
practiced in the lab generalize everywhere: standardize (or, for SGNS, L2-normalize —
you know why) using *training-fold statistics only*, and report across several
training seeds, because embedding runs have real variance and single-run deltas
under a point are noise. This probe protocol will grade every representation for the
rest of the course — GCN activations in Week 6 get the exact same treatment — so the
habits are worth setting now.

**Link prediction.** Score a candidate pair by $\mathbf{z}_u^\top \mathbf{z}_v$ (or
build an edge feature from the pair and classify it). The node2vec paper's Table 1
compared four ways of turning two node vectors into one edge vector — average,
Hadamard (elementwise product), absolute difference, squared difference — and
Hadamard won broadly enough that it became the field's default. It is worth ten
seconds seeing *why* it should: a logistic regression on the Hadamard vector computes

$$
\mathbf{w}^\top(\mathbf{z}_u \odot \mathbf{z}_v) \;=\; \sum_{i=1}^{d} w_i\, z_{u,i}\, z_{v,i}
$$ {#eq-w03-hadamard}

where $\odot$ is the elementwise (Hadamard) product, $z_{u,i}$ is coordinate $i$ of
$u$'s embedding, and $\mathbf{w} \in \mathbb{R}^d$ is the learned classifier weight
vector — so the score is a *weighted* dot product: the plain dot-product scorer with
a learned importance per dimension. (File that shape away: next week an entire KG
model — DistMult — is exactly @eq-w03-hadamard with the weights renamed as a
relation.) This is
the deployment shape of friend suggestion and co-purchase recommendation. But the evaluation has a trap that
publishes wrong numbers every year, so learn the protocol as a reflex:

::: {.callout-important title="Link prediction without lying to yourself" icon="false"}
Held-out edges must be **invisible at every stage**:

1. remove the test edges *before* running any walks — walks that stroll across a
   test edge leak it straight into the similarity counts;
2. sample negative test pairs (non-edges) honestly, and report the
   positives-vs-negatives ranking quality — here the **AUC**, the probability that a
   randomly chosen true edge outscores a randomly chosen non-edge (0.5 = coin-flip,
   1.0 = perfect ranking; Hits@K when Week 12 does this properly);
3. never tune on the test AUC.

In Lab 3 you will run the leaky version and
the clean version side by side: the clean pipeline earns an honest 0.82, while the
leaky one "achieves" a near-perfect 0.997 — seventeen points of pure fiction you will
remember whenever you review a paper.
:::

## 7. The baseline that learns nothing — and the four walls

Before crediting embeddings with magic, meet the baseline every node-classification
result must beat when labels are scarce. Two labeled members, majority-vote flooding,
no vectors anywhere:

{{< include ../assets/d3/w3-labelprop.html >}}

Two labels and two sweeps recover almost the whole split — under strong homophily,
*inference along edges* is devastatingly effective. Label propagation (and its smoothed
descendants) remains the honest baseline: when it matches your embedding pipeline, the
graph's labels were simply easy to spread, and no representation learning was needed.
What it cannot do: produce a score, a feature vector, a ranking, or anything for a node
with no labeled path — the moment the task is not "spread these labels", you need
vectors again.

The widget's majority vote is the coarsest member of a family with real mathematical
depth, and the depth connects straight back to Week 1. The smooth version asks: find
label *scores* $\mathbf{x}$ that (a) equal the known labels on labeled nodes and
(b) minimize $\mathbf{x}^\top \mathbf{L} \mathbf{x}$ — the Laplacian's
disagreement-meter — everywhere else. The solution makes every unlabeled node's score
the *average of its neighbors'* (a harmonic function, the discrete version of heat
settling to equilibrium with the labels as fixed-temperature boundary), and it is a
linear solve, no training. That one idea — *labels should vary smoothly across edges,
and the Laplacian defines smoothly* — resurfaces twice more in this course wearing
better clothes: as the "Correct & Smooth" post-processing that embarrassed several
GNNs on leaderboards ([Huang et al., 2020](https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.13993) — a
Week 3 optional-reading rabbit hole), and inside the GCN
itself, whose propagation step Week 6 will reveal as a learned, feature-aware
relative of exactly this averaging. When someone asks what graph deep learning
actually added, one honest answer is: label propagation, but for *features*, with the
propagation itself trainable.

Now the four walls of everything built today. They are structural — each one is a fact
about the *lookup-table encoder*, not about training quality:

1. **No parameter sharing.** Every node learns its row from scratch. Two structurally
   identical nodes share nothing; regularities of graph structure are re-learned
   $|\mathcal{V}|$ times. (Statistical inefficiency.)
2. **Transductive only.** A node that was not in the table at training time *has no
   embedding* — a new user, a new paper, tomorrow's graph. There is nothing to look
   up. Transductive failure is deployment failure: most production graphs grow every
   hour.
3. **Feature-blind.** Cora's papers *have text*; molecules have atom types; users have
   profiles. The lookup table cannot ingest any of it — the encoder's input is an id.
   All of Lab 2's attribute information is still on the floor.
4. **$O(|\mathcal{V}| \cdot d)$ parameters.** A billion nodes at $d = 128$ in float32
   is half a terabyte of *parameters* — before you store the graph.

The second wall is important enough to deserve its formal name — the exam will use
both words:

::: {#def-w03-transductive .definition name="Transductive vs. inductive"}
A model is **transductive** when it can make predictions only for the exact objects
present at training time; a lookup-table encoder is structurally transductive,
because an unseen node has no row. A model is **inductive** when it can process
objects it never saw during training — the property Week 6's neural encoders buy by
*computing* $\mathbf{z}_u$ from features and neighbors instead of storing it. Read
"transductive" as: the model is a cache of answers, not a function.
:::

Put faces on the walls before generalizing, because each has a canonical victim.
No sharing: a citation network of fresh preprints, where most nodes have degree 1–2 —
each row of the table gets a handful of gradient updates and stays half-random, while
the *pattern* "cites two survey papers → probably an applications paper" exists and
goes unlearned. Transductive: any recommender on day one of a marketing campaign —
the flood of new users is precisely the population the cached table cannot score.
Feature-blind: Cora itself, where two papers with near-identical abstracts sit in
different graph regions and the encoder is *forbidden by construction* from noticing
the abstracts. Parameters: the moment someone says "let's embed all customers" at a
bank — half a terabyte of parameters is an infrastructure project, not a model.

Read the four again and notice they share a single cause: the encoder is a table. The
fix, then, is a different encoder — one that *computes* $\mathbf{z}_u$ from $u$'s
features and neighborhood instead of looking it up. Computed from neighbors means
sharing (one network for all nodes), inductive (new node? run the network),
feature-aware (features are the input), and constant-size. That encoder is the graph
neural network, and Weeks 6–9 are its story.

## Common pitfalls

::: {.callout-warning title="Pitfall 1 · Walking across your test set" icon="false"}
The most common broken graph-ML evaluation in the wild: split edges into train/test,
but run the walks (or compute the PPMI matrix) on the *full* graph. The similarity
counts now contain the answers. Always: remove test edges, *then* walk. If your link
AUC is suspiciously high, this is the first thing to audit — Lab 3 quantifies the
inflation.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Pitfall 2 · Comparing coordinates across runs" icon="false"}
The loss depends on embeddings only through dot products, so any rotation of the whole
cloud is an equally good optimum — coordinates are not identifiable, only geometry is.
Never compare $\mathbf{z}_u$ from two runs dimension-by-dimension, never average
embeddings across runs, never interpret "dimension 7". Within one run, distances and
dot products are meaningful; across runs, only after alignment (orthogonal Procrustes —
mentioned, not examined).
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Pitfall 3 · Shipping a lookup table to a growing graph" icon="false"}
The transductive trap in production: the model works in the notebook, then Monday's
new users have no rows. Teams discover this at deploy time with impressive regularity.
If entities arrive over time, a shallow embedding is a cache, not a model — plan for
recomputation, folding-in heuristics, or an inductive encoder from day one.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Pitfall 4 · Believing the t-SNE plot" icon="false"}
t-SNE/UMAP are for *seeing*, not for *concluding*, and knowing one sentence of their
mechanics tells you which conclusions die: both methods optimize the preservation of
*local neighborhoods* (who is near whom, within a perplexity-sized bubble —
perplexity being t-SNE's neighborhood-size knob) and treat
everything beyond that bubble as "far, don't care." Consequences: within-blob
structure is meaningful-ish; blob *sizes* are artifacts of the density equalization;
distances *between* blobs mean nothing at all; and at some perplexity settings the
methods will happily shatter a continuous manifold into convincing-looking clusters.
Lab 3's protocol: conclusions come from the downstream metric (accuracy, AUC); the
2-D plot is a debugging aid. If the plot looks great and the probe accuracy is
mediocre, believe the probe.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Pitfall 5 · Negatives that are too easy" icon="false"}
Uniform negative sampling mostly draws low-degree nodes (there are many) that the
model easily rejects — training "succeeds" while learning little beyond degree. The
$\deg^{3/4}$ noise distribution is the training-side fix; the evaluation-side twin is
worse: reporting link-prediction metrics against uniformly random non-edges flatters
every model, since real negatives (plausible-but-absent links) are hard. State your
negative distribution when you report results; ask for it when you read them.
:::

[Lab 3](../labs/lab03.qmd) builds the whole pipeline from scratch — no embedding
library anywhere, so that every moving part you just derived has a line of your own
code attached to it — and then measures it honestly: generate walks and windowed pairs on the cast graph (checked against hand
counts); implement the SGNS update in PyTorch and train real embeddings on the karate
club, watching the loss and the faction separation; scale the same code to Cora and
beat Lab 2's 62% baseline with learned vectors; run link prediction both leaky and
clean and put a number on the leak; and close with the t-SNE ritual — plus its
Pitfall-4 disclaimer — on your own trained embeddings.

## Required reading

**1 · Perozzi, Al-Rfou & Skiena — *DeepWalk: Online Learning of Social Representations* (KDD 2014).** [arXiv:1403.6652](https://arxiv.org/abs/1403.6652)

::: {.reading-annotation}
The hijack itself. Read §4 (the pipeline: truncated walks → SkipGram) closely, and
Figure 1 — the karate club embedded in 2D, the exact experiment you ran in this
lecture's Figure 3. Note §3.1's empirical argument that node-visit frequencies follow
the same power law as words: that observation *is* the paper's license to borrow
word2vec. Skim the hierarchical-softmax details (§4.2.2) — modern practice, and this
course, use negative sampling instead.
:::

**2 · Grover & Leskovec — *node2vec: Scalable Feature Learning for Networks* (KDD 2016).** [arXiv:1607.00653](https://arxiv.org/abs/1607.00653)

::: {.reading-annotation}
One change to DeepWalk — the $(p, q)$-biased second-order walk — and a masterclass in
evaluating it. Study Figure 2 and the search-bias equations in §3.2 until you can
predict walk behavior at extreme $p$ and $q$; connect them to homophily vs. structural
equivalence via the Les Misérables case study (Figure 3). Table 1's binary operators
for edge features (Hadamard et al.) are still the standard recipe — Lab 3 uses them.
Skim the parameter-sensitivity plots.
:::

**Also see:** Hamilton, *GRL book*, §3.1–3.3 (neighborhood reconstruction; our
notation follows it) · CS224W, "Node Embeddings".

**Optional:** Tang et al., [LINE](https://arxiv.org/abs/1503.03578) (WWW 2015) — walks
dropped for two explicit objectives (first- and second-order proximity); read as an
alternative similarity design · Qiu et al., [Network Embedding as Matrix
Factorization](https://arxiv.org/abs/1710.02971) (WSDM 2018) — the NetMF derivation
behind @prp-netmf; Table 1 is the paper in one page · Hamilton, Ying & Leskovec,
[Representation Learning on Graphs](https://arxiv.org/abs/1709.05584) (2017) — reread
§2.3's limitations list after this lecture and notice it is §7 in survey form.

## Check your understanding

<details><summary>Q1 · The template — Place these in the encoder/decoder/similarity/loss template: (a) factorizing A with squared error; (b) DeepWalk; (c) LINE's first-order objective (connected nodes should have similar vectors). Which single component changes across all three?</summary>
All three: lookup-table encoder, dot-product-family decoder. (a) $S = \mathbf{A}[u,v]$,
squared-error loss; (b) $S$ = walk co-occurrence counts, softmax/SGNS loss;
(c) $S = \mathbf{A}[u,v]$ again but with a logistic loss on edges. The load-bearing
difference is the **similarity** (and its paired loss) — the encoder and decoder are
commodity parts this week. That is why the framework earns its place: it isolates the
one decision that matters.
</details>

<details><summary>Q2 · Hand computation — The pipeline emits the walk (B, C, E, F) with window w = 1. List every pair in 𝒟, then write out the full SGNS term for the pair (C, E) with k = 2, naming each symbol and stating which vectors receive gradient.</summary>
Pairs (center, context), $w=1$: (B,C), (C,B), (C,E), (E,C), (E,F), (F,E) — six pairs.
For (C,E) with negatives $n_1, n_2 \sim P_n$:
$\log\sigma(\mathbf{z}_C^\top\mathbf{z}_E) + \log\sigma(-\mathbf{z}_C^\top\mathbf{z}_{n_1}) + \log\sigma(-\mathbf{z}_C^\top\mathbf{z}_{n_2})$.
Gradient flows into $\mathbf{z}_C$ (from all three terms), $\mathbf{z}_E$ (pulled
toward $\mathbf{z}_C$), and $\mathbf{z}_{n_1}, \mathbf{z}_{n_2}$ (pushed away). No
other rows of $\mathbf{Z}$ are touched — that locality is the entire point of negative
sampling.
</details>

<details><summary>Q3 · p and q — A barbell graph: two 10-cliques joined by a 6-node path. Task A: embed so the two cliques form two clusters. Task B: embed so the path's bridge nodes cluster with each other. Choose (p, q) regimes for each and justify; state which task the method will do worse at even with ideal settings.</summary>
Task A: low $q$ (DFS-flavored, e.g. $p=4, q=0.25$) — walks range within their side,
co-occurrence = community, cliques separate. Task B wants *structural equivalence*:
high $q$, low $p$ (BFS-flavored) keeps walks local so bridge nodes get
bridge-fingerprint statistics — but the two bridges are far apart and rarely co-occur,
so they cluster only weakly, via similar contexts rather than shared ones. Task B is
the one node2vec does worse at: @prp-netmf says the optimum is a co-occurrence
factorization, and distant role-twins have near-zero co-occurrence. Role embeddings
need different machinery (struc2vec/GraphWave).
</details>

<details><summary>Q4 · The factorization lens — Use the NetMF statement to answer: (a) why does adding a second, disconnected copy of the graph leave every original embedding unchanged? (b) why can increasing d never hurt the training objective but can hurt downstream accuracy?</summary>
(a) Walks never cross between components, so no cross-component pair enters
$\mathcal{D}$: the PMI matrix is block-diagonal and each block factorizes
independently — the copy adds rows but changes no original entries. (Corollary: a node
with no path to labeled data gets an embedding, but one *unconstrained* relative to the
labeled region — compare label propagation, which honestly gives it nothing.)
(b) Larger $d$ can only lower reconstruction error of the shifted-PMI matrix (more
rank), but the tail of that spectrum is walk-sampling noise; fitting it is
memorization, and the downstream classifier inherits the noise. Choosing $d$ is
choosing a rank cutoff — a bias-variance dial, not a "more is better" knob.
</details>

<details><summary>Q5 · The four walls — Match each scenario to the limitation that bites first: (a) a fraud model must score accounts created an hour ago; (b) embeddings for a 2·10⁹-node social graph; (c) two papers with near-identical abstracts get unrelated embeddings; (d) training on a small citation graph overfits although the same architecture worked on a large one.</summary>
(a) transductive-only — new accounts have no row; (b) $O(|\mathcal{V}|d)$ parameters —
a terabyte-scale table; (c) feature-blindness — text never enters the encoder;
(d) no parameter sharing — each node's row is fit independently, so small graphs give
few effective samples per parameter and nothing is amortized across structure. One
cause underneath all four: the encoder is a table, not a function.
</details>

<details><summary>Q6 · Spot the leak — A student splits Cora's edges 90/10, trains node2vec on the full graph "since embeddings are unsupervised anyway", then evaluates dot-product link prediction on the held-out 10%. Name the flaw, predict the direction of the bias, and give the two-line fix.</summary>
The walks crossed the held-out edges, so their endpoints co-occurred in $\mathcal{D}$
— the test answers are inside the similarity statistics ("unsupervised" does not mean
"can't leak"; the graph *is* the label here). Bias: AUC inflated, models ranked by how
well they memorize rather than generalize. Fix: build the train graph *first* (test
edges removed), run all walks and training on it, evaluate on the held-out edges
against honestly sampled non-edges. Lab 3 measures the gap.
</details>

<details><summary>Q7 · Choosing the baseline — For each setting, say whether label propagation or shallow embeddings + classifier is the better first tool, and why: (a) 2 labels per class, strong homophily, one-off analysis; (b) labels needed as features for a downstream ranking model; (c) a heterophilous transaction graph (fraudsters transact with victims); (d) a graph with several components, labels all in one.</summary>
(a) Label propagation — with almost no labels and high homophily it is near-optimal,
free, and has no hyperparameters (today's Figure 4). (b) Embeddings — LP outputs
labels, not vectors; the downstream model needs features. (c) Neither works as-is:
LP's majority vote actively inverts under heterophily (Week 1's Q7), and walk
co-occurrence also encodes "connected ⇒ similar". You need methods that learn the
*sign* of the relation — a Week 7 topic. (d) LP gives the unlabeled components
literally nothing; embeddings give them coordinates, but Q4(a) warns those coordinates
are unanchored to the labeled region — so both need care, and saying *why* for each is
the answer.
</details>

::: {.notions}
Notions introduced this week

- **Encoder–decoder template** (@def-w03-encdec) — encoder, decoder, similarity, loss: the four slots every embedding method fills.
- **Walk corpus** (@alg-w03-corpus) — the multiset $\mathcal{D}$ of (center, context) pairs; all the graph the loss will ever see.
- **Negative sampling** (@def-w03-negsampling) — binary discrimination against $k$ noise draws in place of the full softmax.
- **SGNS update** (@alg-w03-sgns) — one sigmoid pull, $k$ sigmoid pushes; exactly $k+2$ rows touched per pair.
- **Shifted PMI / PPMI** (@eq-w03-netmf) — the matrix SGNS secretly factorizes; PPMI clips the negative entries to zero.
- **node2vec bias $\alpha_{pq}$** (@eq-w03-pq) — the BFS↔DFS dial: $1/p$ back, $1$ sideways, $1/q$ outward.
- **Frozen linear probe** — logistic regression on frozen vectors; measures the representation, not the classifier.
- **Transductive vs. inductive** (@def-w03-transductive) — predictions only for training-time nodes vs. for any node.
- **Label propagation** — majority-vote flooding of known labels along edges; the no-learning baseline.
- **AUC** — the probability that a random positive outranks a random negative; 0.5 is coin-flipping.
:::

## Where this leaves us

You can now learn a vector for anything that sits in a graph — no feature engineering,
just walks, windows, and a sigmoid — and you know precisely what those vectors contain
(co-occurrence, factorized) and what they miss (roles, features, unseen nodes). The
cast graph, the karate club, and Cora have all surrendered their geometry.

Before the cliffhanger, bank the week's transferable skills, because they outlive the
specific method: you can derive a sampled softmax approximation and say what its
fixed point is; you can read any embedding method as a similarity-times-loss choice
and ask "what matrix does it factorize?"; you can design a probe that measures a
representation rather than a classifier; and you carry two permanent leak detectors
(walks over test edges; coordinates across runs). Those four travel to language
models, recommenders, and vision embeddings unchanged — this week was secretly a
course on representation learning that happened to use graphs. And keep the
normalization reflex: a vector's norm and its direction can encode different
things — frequency in one, meaning in the other — so choosing what to normalize
is part of experimental design, not housekeeping.

Close the loop — no notes: the SGNS update's two pushes for one positive pair;
the matrix DeepWalk factorizes, in one phrase; which of $p, q$ drags the walk
home; and the two leak detectors. One minute now beats ten in the exam hall.

But look back at Lab 1's twelve Wikidata triples. *Innopolis University —
located_in — Innopolis. Kazan — capital_of — Tatarstan.* Every edge today was a bare,
anonymous link — while real knowledge comes as **typed, directed facts**, where
*capital_of* and *flows_through* must not embed the same way, and where the interesting
question is not "are these similar?" but "**is this fact true?**" Next week the
decoder grows up: relations become geometric operations — translations, rotations —
vectors start doing algebra, and we can ask a graph to *complete* itself. That is
knowledge graphs, part I — the half of this course's title we have not touched yet.
